name: Steelyard
spatial_setting: a house called the Gildehalla Teutonica, commonly the Steelyard
regulations: instituted for safe trade by land and sea, for the peace of the commonwealth, and for the education of young merchants
profile_summary:
The London Kontor is the only one of the four this corpus can currently describe from a source it has verified. The STILLIARDS text block on the 1593 Civitates London plate calls the Hansa a confederated society of many cities, and states that it holds four emporia, 'which some call Kontore', in which the merchants of the cities reside and carry on their trade. One of them is at London, in a house named the Gildehalla Teutonica, 'commonly called the Steelyard'.

The same block gives the establishment's stated purpose - safe conduct of trade by land and sea, the tranquil peace of the commonwealth, and preserving the modest education of young merchants - and records that it was adorned with the privileges and immunities of many kings and princes, especially of England, France, Denmark and Great Muscovy, and of the dukes of Flanders and Brabant. That list is the privilege-grant model in a contemporary source's own words.

What this profile deliberately does NOT state is when any of it began or ended. The plate describes a condition in 1593; it dates nothing. Status phases, the compound's legal standing under English authority over time, and the commodities traded remain open, and the row stays provisional until they rest on evidence rather than on a single late description.
notes: One of the four Kontore named in KAN-305. Profile content is sourced entirely from the STILLIARDS block at Civitates vol. 1 p. Aa (see evidence.csv, claims hse-claim-hansa-confoederata-societas and hse-claim-four-kontore-attested). Dates, status phases and commodities are still pending by design: a 1593 plate attests a condition, not a chronology.

name: Bruges Kontor
profile_summary:
The Bruges plate of 1593 describes the city as holding the best of urban forms, the circular, well supplied with water and ringed by a double moat - and closes 'florentissimum quondam emporium fuit': it once was a most flourishing emporium.

The tense is the substance. A source printed in 1593 already places Bruges' commercial primacy in the past, which supports the decline narrative without any date having to be asserted for it.

Nothing in the plate identifies the Hanseatic establishment itself, and this corpus must not assume it is visible. The compound's location, legal standing and phases remain open.
notes: One of the four Kontore named in KAN-305. Bruges lacked a single enclosed precinct for much of its history; the spatial_setting field must record that rather than assume a compound, and is left pending because no verified source in this corpus establishes it. Profile content is sourced from Civitates vol. 1 p. 16a (evidence claim hse-claim-bruges-emporium-past-tense).
